articles.body:
Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) plans to introduce a bill Monday that would nullify President Trump’s executive order renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

The one-page “Hands Off Our Great Lakes Act” bill would ensure the executive order “shall have no force or effect” and “restore the name of Lake Ontario,” according to documents obtained by Politico . Dingell confirmed the drafted legislation’s veracity in a Thursday evening post to social platform X.

The Great Lakes are a shared treasure that generations of Americans and Canadians have worked together to protect,” Dingell’s post reads. “That’s why I’m introducing legislation to keep Lake Ontario as Lake Ontario and block President Trump’s idiotic order.”

The Michigan Democrat was an almost immediate critic of Trump’s Thursday decision to formally change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America amid the ongoing trade war between the U.S. and Canada.

Dingell said in a press release Thursday, published before she announced her bill, the lawmaker affirmed that the body of water would “always be Lake Ontario.”

“Canada is not our enemy. It is our neighbor, our ally, and one of Michigan’s most important economic partners. It is a friendship that no stroke of a pen can erase,” Dingell said.

She added, “When President Trump is done doing arts and crafts in the Oval, I’d suggest he turn his attention to his failed economy that is raising costs, eliminating jobs, and leaving working men and women behind.”

The trade war will likely raise costs for American consumers once Canada’s retaliatory tariffs go into effect on Sept. 8. According to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer’s office, goods and services exchanged between the two countries totaled an estimated $872.3 billion in 2025.

The conflict began when Ottawa withdrew from negotiations with Washington, causing the Trump administration to impose 50 percent tariffs on a collection of Canadian goods. In response, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney pledged to match these taxes starting Sept. 8.

After Trump first threatened to rename Lake Ontario Tuesday, Dingell floated instead naming the body of water “Lake Natalie” after longtime White House aide Natalie Harp — a jab based on growing speculation surrounding her work with the president. The Michigan lawmaker joked the move would push the president to “start protecting our Great Lakes.”

Thursday’s executive order came after Trump initially publicly floated changing the name of Lake Ontario earlier this week as a trade war heated up between the U.S. and Canada. Trump told reporters he had thought about renaming the Great Lake for “a long time.”

Over the weekend, trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa boiled over after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney removed negotiators from trade discussions with the Americans.

The fresh tensions follow a pattern of rocky relations between the two North American neighbors, who both border the Great Lakes, during Trump’s second term.

articles.title: Judge blocks Trump’s Postal Service regulation on mail-in ballots
articles.summary: The judge said the regulation is most likely unlawful because the president can’t insert the federal government into elections without Congress’ approval.
articles.body: A federal judge Thursday blocked a Postal Service regulation that would exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections in the latest setback on the issue for President Donald Trump. The recently finalized measure would implement a key provision of Trump’s executive order on mail-in ballots that would add a new level of bureaucracy to the elections process, which is typically administered by states. The executive order directed the U.S. Postal Service to, among other things, track mail-in ballots and potentially reject those submitted by people not on a federal list of eligible voters. The decision by Boston-based U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in one case brought by the League of Women Voters and other groups and another brought by a coalition of states means part of the executive order remains blocked for at least 14 days, with time running out to implement it ahead of the November election. “This rule is a clear attempt by the federal government to interfere in elections it has no power to control,” New York Attorney General Letitia James said in a statement. “Today, a federal court halted it before this administration could wreak havoc on our elections.” Talwani wrote that the regulation is most likely unlawful because the president cannot insert the federal government into elections without the express authorization of Congress. “The court finds plaintiffs likely to succeed on the merits of their claims,” she said. The Trump administration could seek to quickly overturn her decision by rushing to the Supreme Court. Trump often criticizes mail-in ballots, claiming without evidence that there is rampant fraud even though they are widely used by Republicans and Democrats all across the country. Talwani noted in her ruling that the administration had not offered “any evidence regarding fraudulent absentee or mail-in voting.” The government’s interest in “correcting an unsubstantiated problem through likely unconstitutional means is dwarfed by the overwhelming risk of pervasive disenfranchisement,” she added. Directly addressing the short time frame ahead of the election, Talwani said states “have neither time nor funds” to meet the necessary requirements, including updating election management systems and training staff members. Based on the evidence before her, states’ compliance with what the Trump administration is asking of them before the 2026 midterms would be “practically impossible,” Talwani wrote. In a separate decision Wednesday, Talwani lifted an earlier injunction she had imposed that blocked vital elements of Trump’s executive order in the case. It is a different injunction from the one the Supreme Court lifted Monday in a similar case brought by California and 22 other states. Talwani is overseeing both cases. The Supreme Court found that Talwani had acted too hastily in ruling on the executive order but did not weigh in on whether the underlying proposal or the Postal Service regulation is lawful. While the Postal Service regulation is now blocked, a provision of the executive order requiring the Department of Homeland Security to compile lists of eligible voters and send them to states remains in effect.

articles.body:
A Florida grand jury found Gov. Ron DeSantis’s (R-Fla.) administration “misappropriated” a payment from a Medicaid settlement into the Hope Florida Foundation — an organization “championed” by first lady Casey DeSantis.

The grand jury argued the $10 million transfer was “part of a sophisticated scheme to fund political activities,” according to a copy of the sealed grand jury report obtained by CBS News Miami .

The money was originally part of a $67 million settlement agreement against the state’s largest Medicaid contractor, Centene, with $10 million going to Hope Florida as a “donation.”

The donated money was meant “to be a community-based welfare program that serves as a cost-efficient alternative to government assistance programs.”

The report found it was instead used by organizations that helped campaign against a Florida ballot measure that would have legalized recreational marijuana in 2024.

The arrangement reportedly funneled the payment through the charity connected to Hope Florida and was eventually sent to two nonprofit groups involved in the campaign against the ballot measure.

“Despite our finding that the money was misappropriated, we find insufficient evidence to charge anyone criminally,” the report concluded. “Nobody will take responsibility for deciding the $10 million of taxpayer money would go to Hope Florida… or had any memory of who made it.”

The grand jury implicated Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), who was attorney general at the time and not called to testify, was aware of the plan to divert the payment and “authorized” her former chief deputy, John Guard, to sign the settlement agreement.

Moody is up for reelection this year after being appointed by DeSantis to take over Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s seat.

The Chief of Staff for DeSantis, James Uthmeier, was also found to be “in a position of authority over those involved in settling.”

“Testimony identified him as having involvement in directing the money after it went to Hope Florida. Testimony also revealed that Mr. Uthmeier’s Keep Florida Clean, a political action committee, was the prime recipient of the majority of the $10 million taxpayer funds,” the grand jury wrote.

The Florida governor has maintained other 2025 probes into the scheme as part of a “manufactured” smear campaign against him and his wife.

“It was all political,” DeSantis told reporters in 2025. “People smear what they fear. If Hope Florida represents a threat to their world view, they’re going to go after it.”

articles.body:
A federal judge in Boston has again blocked the Trump administration from moving forward with new mail-in voting restrictions ahead of the November midterms for at least another two weeks.

Judge Indira Talwani ruled Thursday night that a group of blue states and private voting rights groups were likely to succeed in their claims that the U.S. Postal Service rule is unconstitutional, and that the agency lacked authority to issue it.

The temporary restraining order blocks enforcement of the rule for 14 days, which extends beyond when some of the first states begin sending out absentee and overseas ballots.

“Based on the record presently before the court, Plaintiff States face irreparable harm where they are required to comply with a likely unconstitutional regulation for which compliance is practically impossible as to the 2026 midterm elections, now little more than two months away,” Talwani wrote.

The Postal Service published its final rule in the Federal Register Wednesday, which requires that mail ballots have certain designs and specifications, including a unique logo and barcode with an embedded ZIP code.

It also requires state and local election officials to submit lists of eligible voters to the agency before it mails ballots.

The rule implements some of the provisions President Trump had directed as part of a March executive order, as his administration works to exert more control over federal elections. The president has often criticized mail-in voting as ripe for fraud, despite little evidence to support the claim.

The Supreme Court, over the dissent of the three liberal justices, held on Monday that a previous blue-state challenge to Trump’s executive order was brought prematurely and lifted the prior injunction.

That decision prompted Talwani, an Obama appointee, to lift her remaining nationwide injunction on Wednesday despite finding that the administration had violated her order.

A group of Democratic-led states, the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts and other groups promptly filed new challenges to the rule this week, arguing that it interferes with states’ authority to administer its own elections and risks disenfranchising eligible voters.

Talwani agreed, writing that there was an “overwhelming risk” to Americans who need access to mail ballots to vote that warranted the court’s intervention.
